# Workflow Dependency Lockfiles with gh actions-lock

After this page you can generate and maintain a `.github/workflows/actions.lock` lockfile with the `gh actions-lock` extension, review lockfile diffs like any other dependency change, check coverage in a pre-commit hook and in CI, and handle upstream refs that move.

## Thesis

GitHub Actions tags are mutable. Pinning each `uses:` line to a full commit SHA closes that gap for the actions you name, but it is tedious, hides the version unless you annotate it, and does nothing for the actions a composite action uses internally. Workflow dependency lockfiles (public preview on October 14, 2026, generally available on October 28, 2026) move the pins into one file, `.github/workflows/actions.lock`, which records a commit SHA, owner ID and repository ID for every direct and transitive action. Your workflows keep readable version refs, and every change to what runs shows up as a reviewable diff.

## The problem: tag mutability in action workflows

In GitHub Actions, workflow steps reference external actions using ref strings such as `uses: actions/checkout@v4` or `uses: owner/repo@v1`. Because Git tags and branches are mutable pointers, an upstream maintainer or an attacker who compromises an upstream repository can move a tag to point to a malicious commit.

This supply chain vulnerability was demonstrated in March 2025 during the `tj-actions/changed-files` compromise, where mutable tags were redirected to malicious commits. Standard tag-based references execute whatever commit the remote tag references at the moment the workflow job starts. Hand-pinning direct actions to a 40-character SHA (for example, `uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683`) mitigates direct tag tampering, but it introduces developer friction, hides version numbers unless manually annotated in comments, and completely ignores nested dependencies within composite actions.

## What `.github/workflows/actions.lock` records

A workflow dependency lockfile is a repository-wide document stored at `.github/workflows/actions.lock`. Generated by the official `gh actions-lock` CLI extension, it records top-level metadata alongside two key sections:

1. **`workflows`**: Maps each workflow file path (such as `.github/workflows/ci.yml`) to the list of action references it depends on.
2. **`dependencies`**: Maps each canonical action reference to its cryptographic commit hash (`sha1-<40 hex chars>`), original repository owner ID, and repository ID.

The numeric `owner_id` and `repo_id` fields identify the repository itself, not just its name. If a name you depend on is deleted and re-created, or taken over by someone else (repo-jacking), the IDs no longer match what you locked, so a changed ID in a lockfile diff is a signal to stop and investigate.

Unlike hand-pinned workflow files, the extension pins "every direct and transitive dependency" (in the words of its own help text), including actions that a composite action calls.

## Generating the lockfile

To generate and manage lockfiles, install or upgrade the GitHub CLI extension:

```bash
gh extension install github/gh-actions-lock
gh extension upgrade gh-actions-lock
```

The sample repository contains a single workflow file defining a Python testing pipeline.

<!-- file: ci.yml -->
```yaml
name: ci
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v6
        with:
          python-version: "3.14"
      - run: python -m pytest -q
```

Check the installed extension and CLI versions:

```bash
gh actions-lock --version; gh --version
```

The command above produces the following output:

```text
actions-lock version v0.4.1
gh version 2.102.0 (2026-09-30)
```

Running `gh actions-lock --no-fix` against an unpinned repository performs a read-only scan of all workflows under `.github/workflows/`.

```bash
gh actions-lock --no-fix
```

The command above produces the following output:

```text
Scanning 1 workflow
1 of 1 workflow failed
✗ Not pinned actions/checkout@v5
  used in workflow but not pinned in lockfile (actions/checkout@v5)
  see: https://github.com/github/gh-actions-lock/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#not-pinned
  ↳ .github/workflows/ci.yml
✗ Not pinned actions/setup-python@v6
  used in workflow but not pinned in lockfile (actions/setup-python@v6)
  see: https://github.com/github/gh-actions-lock/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md#not-pinned
  ↳ .github/workflows/ci.yml
Re-run without --no-fix to apply fixes.
Run log: ~/.cache/gh-actions-lock/logs/run-20261103-121034-1362276858.json
exit status: 1
```

To onboard all workflows in `.github/workflows/` and write the lockfile, execute `gh actions-lock` without `--no-fix`. The `--no-interactive` flag ensures non-interactive execution:

```bash
gh actions-lock --no-interactive
```

The command above produces the following output:

```text
Scanning 1 workflow
Planning pins
Pinned 2 actions across 1 workflow
  actions/checkout@v5.1.0 (fbc6f39)
    └─ .github/workflows/ci.yml
  actions/setup-python@v6.3.0 (ece7cb0)
    └─ .github/workflows/ci.yml
exit status: 0
```

Running `gh actions-lock` rewrites the workflow file references: partial semver tags (such as `@v5` or `@v6`) are automatically narrowed to the highest matching full semver tag (such as `@v5.1.0` or `@v6.3.0`) without changing the target commit. Branch names and non-version tags are never narrowed. To disable semver narrowing, pass `--no-narrow`.

Inspect the modified workflow file with `git diff`:

```bash
git diff .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

The command above produces the following output:

```text
diff --git a/.github/workflows/ci.yml b/.github/workflows/ci.yml
index 52a1a07..48ce310 100644
--- a/.github/workflows/ci.yml
+++ b/.github/workflows/ci.yml
@@ -6,8 +6,8 @@ jobs:
   test:
     runs-on: ubuntu-latest
     steps:
-      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
-      - uses: actions/setup-python@v6
+      - uses: actions/checkout@v5.1.0
+      - uses: actions/setup-python@v6.3.0
         with:
           python-version: "3.14"
       - run: python -m pytest -q
```

Now inspect the generated `.github/workflows/actions.lock`:

```bash
cat .github/workflows/actions.lock
```

The command above produces the following output:

```text
# This file is machine-generated by `gh actions-lock`.
# Do not edit by hand; run `gh actions-lock` to update.
# Docs: https://gh.io/actions-lockfile
version: 'v0.0.3'
workflows:
    '.github/workflows/ci.yml':
        - 'actions/checkout@v5.1.0'
        - 'actions/setup-python@v6.3.0'
dependencies:
    'actions/checkout@v5.1.0':
        ref: 'v5.1.0'
        commit: 'sha1-fbc6f3992d24b796d5a048ff273f7fcc4a7b6c09'
        owner_id: 44036562
        repo_id: 197814629
    'actions/setup-python@v6.3.0':
        ref: 'v6.3.0'
        commit: 'sha1-ece7cb06caefa5fff74198d8649806c4678c61a1'
        owner_id: 44036562
        repo_id: 192625525
```

The lockfile begins with machine-generated header comments, specifies schema version `v0.0.3`, maps `.github/workflows/ci.yml` to its dependencies, and records exact SHA-1 hashes and repository IDs under `dependencies`.

## Reviewing lockfile changes

Lockfile reviews should be part of standard pull request auditing. When inspecting a diff in `.github/workflows/actions.lock`:

- **Changed `commit` hash**: Indicates an action dependency bump. Verify the upstream release notes or commit log to confirm the code change is intended.
- **Changed `owner_id` or `repo_id`**: Indicates that the underlying GitHub repository object has changed. This occurs when an owner renames an account, deletes and re-creates a repository, or transfers ownership. Treat any unexpected ID change as a potential repository-jacking attempt and investigate upstream ownership before merging.

Never edit `.github/workflows/actions.lock` by hand. Always update it using `gh actions-lock`.

## Keeping lockfiles current

As actions publish new releases, lockfile entries must be systematically updated.

### Dependabot integration

When Dependabot is configured for GitHub Actions, it detects onboarded workflows. When Dependabot updates an action version in an onboarded workflow, it automatically updates the corresponding lockfile entry in `.github/workflows/actions.lock` within the same pull request. For non-onboarded workflows, Dependabot modifies only the workflow YAML.

### Updating moved tags with `--relock`

When an upstream maintainer updates a branch (such as `main`) or a partial semver tag (such as `v3`), the existing lockfile retains its previously pinned commit, and `gh actions-lock` outputs a ref-moved warning. After auditing upstream changes, update the pinned commit to the latest tag target:

```bash
gh actions-lock --relock
```

If a full version tag (such as `v3.1.0`) is moved upstream, `gh actions-lock` reports an error because full version tags are expected to be immutable. Resolving this requires reviewing the upstream release and either running `gh actions-lock --relock` or updating the `uses:` reference in the workflow.

### Handling rewritten history with `--accept-moved`

If upstream repository history is rewritten (for example, via a force-push) such that a previously locked commit is no longer reachable in the remote repository's Git graph, `gh actions-lock` flags a severe verification error. Running `--relock` alone will not resolve a missing commit error.

After verifying that the history change is benign and authorized, accept the new commit point:

```bash
gh actions-lock --accept-moved
```

::: {.callout-warning}
Don't use `--accept-moved` in automation. It re-resolves pins whose history changed, which is exactly the situation a human should review first.
:::

## Verifying lockfiles in CI and pre-commit

Lockfile compliance should be validated automatically at two boundaries: local developer workstations and remote continuous integration runners.

### Remote CI verification: `gh actions-lock --verify`

In CI, use `gh actions-lock --verify`. It is a frozen check: it runs the same checks as the default mode, with network access, but writes nothing, and it fails if the lockfile is incomplete or if the runner would reject a pin. A clean run exits with status 0.

Execute verification against the repository:

```bash
gh actions-lock --verify
```

The command above produces the following output:

```text
Scanning 1 workflow
All 1 workflow valid
exit status: 0
```

For custom reporting pipelines, structured JSON output can be generated using `--json`:

```bash
gh actions-lock --no-fix --json=valid,findings
```

### Local offline verification: `--verify-local`

The `--verify-local` flag performs a local coverage check without network access, authentication tokens, or file modifications. It is designed for git pre-commit hooks to ensure developers do not commit modified workflow files without updating `.github/workflows/actions.lock`.

To test offline verification, simulate adding an unpinned `actions/cache@v4` step to `.github/workflows/ci.yml` without updating the lockfile, then execute `--verify-local`:

```bash
gh actions-lock --verify-local
```

The command above produces the following output:

```text
1 of 1 workflow failed: 1 not-pinned
Run without --verify-local to resolve and pin missing actions.
exit status: 1
```

The run exits with status 1 because `actions/cache@v4` has no lockfile entry. Because `--verify-local` makes no network calls and needs no authentication, it suits a pre-commit hook. It only checks that every action ref has an entry. It does not check that the entries are trustworthy, so keep `gh actions-lock --verify` in CI as well.

## Local actions and reusable workflows

Actions referenced within workflows follow specific lockfile scoping rules depending on how they are referenced:

- **Local path actions (`uses: ./.github/actions/build`)**: the extension never follows or locks a `./` action. A `./` path runs whatever is checked out in the runner's workspace, so there is nothing stable to pin. If such an action itself uses other actions, the extension reports a `local-action` error and writes nothing.
- **Same-repository actions (`uses: $/.github/actions/build`)**: a `$/` reference runs your repository's own action at the workflow's own commit, so it is pinned by construction and the actions it uses can be locked. `--migrate-local-actions` rewrites `./` references to `$/` in your workflows and in-repo `action.yml` files. `--ignore-local-actions` keeps the `./` form and reports it as a warning instead.
- **Reusable workflows in another repository (`uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/reusable.yml@v1`)**: the reusable workflow's own dependencies are covered by the lockfile of the repository where it is defined, not by yours. For full coverage, that repository needs its own lockfile.

## Organization allowlists

A repository, organization or enterprise can be set to allow only specified actions. Once a workflow is onboarded, that allowlist is checked against the locked commit SHAs instead of tags, because a tag can be moved but a locked SHA cannot. An allowlist entry pinned to a tag, such as `actions/checkout@v6`, no longer matches. Use a wildcard or the full commit SHA instead, and check the allowlist before you commit the lockfile.

::: {.callout-note}
**Not run here.** The sample repository in this chapter is local only: it was never pushed, and the workflow never ran on a runner. Making the lockfile mandatory is an administrator policy, described in GitHub's "Enforcing lockfiles for action dependencies" documentation (see Sources); it was not configured here.
:::

## Comparison: Lockfiles vs. manual SHA pinning

| Feature / Dimension | Manual SHA Pinning (`uses: action@SHA # v1`) | Workflow Lockfile (`actions.lock`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Workflow readability** | Low (workflow files filled with 40-char hashes) | High (clean semver or branch refs in YAML) |
| **Transitive dependencies** | Not covered (a composite action's own `uses:` lines still resolve its tags) | Pinned (direct and transitive) |
| **Repository identity** | Not recorded | `owner_id` and `repo_id` recorded per dependency |
| **Updates** | Dependabot or hand edits | Dependabot updates the entry in the same PR; `--relock` for moved refs |
| **Pre-commit check** | Your own script | `gh actions-lock --verify-local` (offline) |
| **Semver narrowing** | Manual | Automatic on onboarding (disable via `--no-narrow`) |

## Common mistakes

- **Editing `.github/workflows/actions.lock` manually**: Hand-editing risks corrupting schema format, `sha1-` prefixes, or numeric `owner_id` mapping. Always use `gh actions-lock` or `gh actions-lock --relock`.
- **Using `--accept-moved` in CI scripts**: Automating `--accept-moved` disables tag-tampering protections across your build pipeline. Restrict `--accept-moved` to manual developer invocations after security review.
- **Expecting local relative actions (`./`) to lock**: `gh actions-lock` skips `./` relative paths. Migrate relative paths to `$/` syntax using `--migrate-local-actions` if root commit pinning is required.
- **Forgetting transitive lockfiles in reusable workflows**: A caller workflow does not lock internal steps of a remote reusable workflow. Ensure external repositories hosting reusable workflows maintain their own `.github/workflows/actions.lock`.
- **Retaining tag-only entries in organization allowlists**: Enforcement policies check resolved commit SHAs once lockfiles are present. Update allowlist rules to accept SHA patterns to prevent broken CI runs.

## Exercises

1. Install `gh actions-lock` and execute `gh actions-lock --no-fix` on an existing workspace. Identify all unpinned actions reported by the scan.
2. Run `gh actions-lock` to generate `.github/workflows/actions.lock`. Compare the workflow file before and after to observe how version tags were narrowed.
3. Configure a pre-commit hook in your local Git repository that executes `gh actions-lock --verify-local`. Add a step using an unpinned action to a workflow and confirm the hook blocks the commit.
4. Add a CI job that runs `gh actions-lock --verify`, then open a pull request that bumps an action without regenerating the lockfile and watch the check fail.

## Summary

- GitHub Actions lockfiles (`.github/workflows/actions.lock`) pin every action your workflows run and turn each change into a reviewable diff.
- The `gh actions-lock` extension scans `.github/workflows/`, pins direct and transitive dependencies to commit SHAs, and narrows partial version refs to full semver tags.
- Lockfiles track immutable `owner_id` and `repo_id` metadata to prevent repository-jacking attacks.
- Verification is split into fast offline local checks (`--verify-local`) for pre-commit hooks and full network checks (`--verify`) for CI pipelines.
- Updates are handled via Dependabot PRs, `gh actions-lock --relock`, and controlled manual review with `--accept-moved`.
